note: Restricts to studies reporting actual safety outcomes rather than model accuracy, and finds no standardised benchmark exists.
title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Patient Safety Outcomes: Systematic Literature Review

reading.body:
This review restricts itself to studies reporting actual measured safety outcomes, rather than model accuracy alone, and finds that no standardized benchmark for that outcome currently exists.

The absence of a standardized safety benchmark is the paper's central finding, and it is a gap rather than a result. It means that two AI systems each reporting strong safety outcomes may not be comparable to each other at all, since they were likely measured against different, unstandardized criteria.

The review does not propose the standardized benchmark it says is missing, only documents that the field lacks one.

explain_beginner: Researchers examined studies about how artificial intelligence helps keep patients safe in hospitals and clinics. They found fifty-three studies showing that AI systems can catch medical errors, identify high-risk patients, and prevent medication problems. However, the studies used different methods to measure success, making it hard to compare results. The review shows AI has real promise for patient safety, but hospitals need better ways to test these systems before widely adopting them.
explain_business: AI applications can meaningfully improve patient safety through better error detection and medication management, representing valuable risk mitigation opportunities. However, organizations should recognize that existing published systems lack standardized evaluation metrics, making it difficult to assess which solutions deliver genuine clinical value. Before implementing AI systems, executives should prioritize vendors demonstrating real-world validation data and ensuring solutions have been tested in actual clinical environments rather than relying solely on algorithm accuracy metrics.
explain_practitioner: This systematic review analyzed fifty-three quantitative studies integrating machine learning and natural language processing for patient safety outcomes between 2009 and 2019. Studies focused on three areas: clinical alarms using decision trees, clinical reports using support vector machines, and drug safety using decision trees. Key findings revealed that while AI-enabled decision support systems improved error detection and patient stratification, significant heterogeneity existed in both AI methodology and performance reporting. Critically, no standardized evaluation benchmark was identified, limiting cross-study comparison and clinical validation.
